text: Vasha stands on the weathered wooden railing of the dock at Frosthollow, his talons curling around the salt-bleached planks. The evening wind catches his breast feathers, ruffling the dense white down that insulates his broad chest, and he shifts his weight, the boards groaning faintly beneath him. His head turns in a slow, deliberate arc, those piercing blue eyes sweeping the harbor — scanning the last fishing boats pulling into port, the gulls wheeling overhead, the lantern light beginning to glow in the windows of the cliff-face nest-houses. The faintest edge of gray darkens the barbs of his primary feathers where they fold against his back, barely visible unless the light catches them just so, and the black crescents bordering his facial disc frame his disc like a mask, giving his expression a quiet intensity. His beak, dark as polished obsidian, rests closed, though his nostrils flare slightly with each breath, tasting the brine and woodsmoke of the harbor air. At three feet and five inches, he is not the largest owl-folk in Frosthollow, but his wingspan stretches nearly eight feet when fully outstretched, a fact the dock workers have learned to respect whenever he launches from this very railing. Right now he is still, watching, waiting — a pale shape against the darkening northern sky.

text:
Vasha stands on the weathered wooden railing of the post office's upper balcony, his talons gripping the edge with a quiet, practiced ease. The late afternoon wind ruffles the long white feathers of his breast and stomach, and he turns his head slowly, those piercing blue eyes scanning the rooftops and chimneys of Frosthollow below. His ears — barely visible beneath the pale down of his facial disc — twitch at the sound of gulls wheeling overhead.

He is enormous by any standard, his broad body and thick neck giving him a solid, grounded presence even at rest. Nearly white from head to tail, he catches the gray-pink light of the setting sun, the faintest bars of gray and black visible only when his wings shift and the primary feathers spread wide. His wingspan, folded now, still drapes past either side of the railing.

In his left talon, he holds a leather pouch sealed with wax — a parcel he picked up from the sorting room below. It is cinched tight and light enough that he could carry it cross-country without effort. His black beak rests against it loosely, waiting.

He has been a postal carrier for eleven years now. His gaze drifts to the harbor, where the fishing boats are pulling in, and something in his stillness suggests he is thinking of his mother.

text:
Vasha stands at the edge of the cliff, his boots planted in the short grass, his hands tucked into the pockets of his coat. The wind presses the fabric against his lean frame, and he tilts his chin up, letting the cold air fill his lungs. His dark eyes track a hawk wheeling far below the cloudline — not with urgency, but with the patient attention of someone who has learned that the world reveals itself only to those who wait.

He does not speak. He rarely does, not because he has nothing to say, but because the silence around him feels like a living thing, textured and full. He has noticed the way the light bends through the mist rolling off the northern coast, the way it turns the sea into something silver and unreachable. He has noticed everything — the gulls banking in formation, the erosion along the stone face below, the single wildflower pushing through a crack in the rock.

His jaw tightens, almost imperceptibly. Somewhere beneath that watchful stillness, beneath the careful cataloguing of detail, there is a pull he has never named aloud. It lives in his chest like weather — restless, directional, pointed always toward the horizon.

He exhales slowly, and the breath becomes visible in the cold air, dissolving into nothing.

text:
Vasha stands at the edge of the dock, his boots planted where the weathered planks meet the sky. The wind pulls at his dark hair, and he lets it. His grey eyes follow the gulls not because he means to, but because his gaze always drifts upward eventually—tracking the way their wings catch the light, the angle at which they bank toward the open sea.

He folds his arms across his chest. A habit. A wall built from years of learning that people hear words the moment they leave your mouth, but never quite hear the silence before them.

Today, the northern horizon is a pale bruise of cloud and distance, and something in it pulls at him the way it always does—a quiet, aching gravity that has nothing to do with falling. He breathes in the salt air and holds it, as though he could keep the ocean inside himself.

His hands are steady. His expression is still. But beneath that stillness, there is a restless thing that watches the horizon the way a bird watches an open window.
